newsitem.title: USA: U.S. corp bonds rally with Treas, endure selling.
newsitem.headline: U.S. corp bonds rally with Treas, endure selling.

text.p: U.S. corporate high-grade bonds weathered profit-taking in the face of rallying U.S. Treasuries and spreads widened only marginally across some sectors into the close, traders said.
"People were tied up with some selling this morning but I didn't really see things widening," one trader said. "Trades were fairly firm throughout."
Meanwhile, some large new issues hit the investment grade and high-yield primaries in bids to capitalize on the sudden drop in rates.

Long U.S. Treasuries embarked more than one point gains after the Labor Department said the overall and core components of its Consumer Price Index rose 0.1 percent in August. Economists in a Reuters poll expected both numbers to post gains of 0.2 percent.
Adding to the fervor, retail sales in August were also weak. The government said sales were up 0.2 percent for the month against forecasts for a 0.7 percent jump.
The benchmark 30-year bond was quoted up 1 15/32 at 97-14/32 to yield 6.95 percent at 1530 EDT/1930 GMT.

Back in the corporate arena, dealers were busied with large institutional bid lists with paper concentrated in the utility sector. Wire reports indicated a plethora of Lockheed Martin debt out for sale.
Elsewhere, the $7 billion merger of Gillette Co and Duracell International Inc was considered a non-event to corporate debt players.

The two companies announced the merger late Thursday. Gillette said it will issue about 108 million shares in the stock transaction, in which Duracell stockholders will receive 0.904 share of Gillette for each Duracell share owned.

Corporate traders qualified outstanding Gillette debt as "museum pieces" and rarely trades. According to Standard & Poor's Bond Guide for August, the firm has three outstanding note issues due in 1996, 2003 and 2005.
Duracell International's last long-term debt issue, $400 million 13.50 percent debt of 2000, was called in September of 1991, one source said.

High-grade new issues included $150 million May Department Stores Co notes due 2011, priced via lead manager Morgan Stanley & Co. The A2/single-A rated notes were given a 7.45 percent coupon and priced to yield 7.481 percent.
Turning to the high-yield sector, traders quoted the entire market up one point in brisk activity. While there were few outperformers, one head trader said "the whole market was on fire today."
Reflecting the grab-fest, First Nationwide Escrow Corp's $575 million 144A senior subordinated notes priced on Friday traded up from par to 102 in the aftermarket, a dealer said.
The deal was also increased in size by $50 million due to strong investor demand, accorinding to one market source.
First Nationwide's notes, rated Ba3/single-B, are due in 2002 and were priced at par with a 10.625 percent coupon. They are non-callable for four and 1/4 years.
Looking ahead, long Treasury yields inside seven percent should breathe new life into corporate issuers, syndicate managers said.
High-yield issues include more paper in an already burgeoning telecommunication sector, one high yield analyst said, including deals from Sygnet Wireless and Gray Communications.
Also, a source said Bankers Trust will price a $150 million PIK preferred issue for high-yield investors.
